summary.text: Carbon capture and storage (CCS) separates carbon dioxide from a large source such as a gas processing plant and moves it to long-term storage, typically in a deep geological formation.
About 80% of captured CO₂ is pumped into partly depleted oil reservoirs to extract more oil, which is why it is also called CCUS.
As of 2024 it ran at 44 plants catching about a thousandth of global CO₂ emissions, while cheaper options like solar and wind cut air pollution far more.

items.prompt: Captured CO₂ from a gas plant is sold to an oil company. What is it most likely used for?

options.label: Making fizzy drinks for sale
Injecting into old oil fields to get more oil out
Turning into plastic packaging
Feeding greenhouses to grow crops

items.explain: Around 80% of captured CO₂ goes to enhanced oil recovery, where it is injected into partly depleted reservoirs to extract more oil.

items.prompt: A power plant adds CCS equipment. What happens to the amount of fuel it burns to run?

options.label: It falls, since the plant runs cleaner
It stays exactly the same
It goes up, because capture uses energy
It drops to zero once storage begins

items.explain: Plants with CCS need more energy to operate, so they typically burn additional fossil fuel.

items.prompt: A company captures CO₂ and turns it into fuel that is later burned in trucks. Why does this not count as CCS?

Fuel making is banned for captured gas
The CO₂ was not captured from a factory
Trucks run on electricity instead

items.explain: CCS requires long-term storage, and products such as fuel release CO₂ again when burned.

About one-tenth

items.explain: Solar, wind, electrification and public transit are less expensive than CCS and much more effective at reducing air pollution.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Carbon capture and storage, or CCS, separates carbon dioxide from an industrial plant or a natural source before it escapes into the air, then moves it somewhere it can be kept for a long time. The CO₂ is taken from a large point source, like a natural gas processing plant. It is usually put away in a deep geological formation underground.

paragraphs.heading: Mostly used for oil
paragraphs.text: About 80% of the CO₂ captured each year goes to enhanced oil recovery (EOR): it is pumped into partly emptied oil fields to push out more oil, and most of it then stays underground. Because the gas is used as well as stored, the process is also called carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS). Around 1% of captured CO₂ becomes feedstock for fertilizer, fuels and plastics. Turning CO₂ into fuel or fertilizer does not count as CCS, since those products give the CO₂ back when burned or used.

paragraphs.heading: From gas fields to climate tool
paragraphs.text: Oil and gas companies were using the steps behind CCS by the mid-20th century. A method for stripping CO₂ out of raw natural gas was patented in 1933, and in 1972 American oil companies found that CO₂ could be used profitably for EOR. Gas processors in Texas then began selling their captured CO₂ to nearby oil producers. In 1977 the Italian physicist Cesare Marchetti suggested CCS could cut emissions from coal power plants and refineries, and from the 1980s, especially the 2000s, it was discussed as a way to reduce greenhouse gases.

paragraphs.heading: How much it does today
paragraphs.text: As of 2024, CCS ran at 44 plants around the world, together catching about one-thousandth of global CO₂ emissions. Roughly 90% of those operations involved the oil and gas industry. A 2022 review found that around 70% of announced projects had not materialized, and in the electricity sector the failure rate was above 98%. Some large projects have stored far less CO₂ than planned, and nearly every project running today has received some financial support from governments.

paragraphs.heading: Costs and doubts
paragraphs.text: A plant with CCS needs extra energy to run, so it usually burns more fossil fuel, adding pollution from extracting and transporting that fuel. How well CCS works depends on how much CO₂ the plant actually captures, the energy CCS itself uses, leaks, and business or technical problems that stop plants running as designed. Solar and wind power, electrification and public transit cost less and cut air pollution far more. Many environmental groups see CCS as unproven, costly and a distraction that prolongs fossil fuel dependence, and whether using CO₂ to pump more oil helps the climate is still disputed.

paragraphs.heading: Where it might fit
paragraphs.text: CCS could still play a critical but limited part in cutting emissions. Given its cost, it is expected to be most useful in niches such as heavy industry and retrofitting existing plants. Alongside deep, lasting cuts in natural gas use, it can lower emissions from gas processing. It is also part of bioenergy with carbon capture and storage, which under some conditions can take carbon out of the atmosphere.
